rationale: Code-mandated recurring inspections with A-level licensing/operator evidence; light OSFM license in 1-3 months. Economics (per-unit pricing, route contribution) are analyst estimates. ~184 licensed competitors incl. Cintas bundles; density takes years. Realistic yr3-5 FCF ~$100-200k with 2-3 techs. Statute sunset 2028 unresolved.
red_flags: Per-unit pricing and route contribution are [E] with no primary pricing
300-800 accounts in 3 yrs via canvassing is an assumption

rationale: Essential consumables with Census-level margin data (23.9% GM, ~6% op margin) but that is incumbent economics; newcomer lacks rebates/volume pricing. Commodity vs Bunzl/Imperial Dade/Amazon with weak wedge. Receivables, inventory and dispenser capex depress ROIC (~35-55%). Delegable distribution roles; roll-up/exit option real.
red_flags: Incumbent margins used; new-entrant GM could fall below 20%

rationale: No pricing or demand evidence (single Census source); founder lacks trade estimating skill. Crowded by offshore shops and AI takeoff software (self-serve substitution risk cuts against the service). Asset-light and fast cash, but commoditized and construction-cyclical; realistic FCF ~$50-80k.
red_flags: Same AI that enables it lets subs self-serve

rationale: Mandated semiannual inspections, reachable buyers, low capital; but standalone ceiling modest, restaurant churn/bad debt high, and manufacturer authorization (parts access) unverified and possibly the binding gate. Pricing is analyst estimate. Better as add-on to extinguisher route than standalone.

Dense Chicago logistics base and real cost-per-load wedge with equipment service, but commodity products vs Uline/consolidators, resin price swings, net-30-60 terms and bulky inventory. Incumbent ~6% op margin; newcomer lower. ROIC ~30-60% once scaled; customer concentration risk.
red_flags: Supplier pricing for new distributor unknown

rationale: Real need but Illinois-only, contested by entrenched lien software (Levelset/Procore) and law firms. Preparing lien claims for others risks unauthorized practice of law; attorney fee-splitting limits. Missed deadlines create heavy liability. No spend evidence; stated ceiling ~$10k/mo.

Mandated annual tests drive inbound demand, but founder cannot test (needs licensed plumber-CCCDI; plumber license needs 4-yr apprenticeship). Scarce, costly licensed labor on $75-200 tickets plus price competition from any plumber compress margins. Payroll precedes density. Pricing/volume are estimates.
red_flags: Margin viability depends on hiring scarce CCCDI plumbers
Plumbing contractor registration requirements on firm

rationale: Founder's lab background helps, but universities are locked into Fisher/VWR contracts and Chicago startup cluster is small and price-shops Amazon. Only incumbent (Avantor) economics cited; author's own yr3 range starts at $0. Slow university AP, private-label quality risk, biotech funding cycles.

Founder can build it cheaply, but the underlying data is free and public; willingness to pay is unproven and national lead databases exist. Stated ceiling ~$5k/mo; trivially copied; seasonal contractor churn. Better as an internal lead tool than a business.

Strong recurring, health-code-driven demand; Rollins commercial GM 52.8% and many small IL operators show a viable small-start model. Founder can certify in months; public CDPH pest-violation data gives a prospect list. Crowded with nationals/independents; tech quality and retention decide churn. Pricing is estimated; consolidator exit plausible.

Census 4.5% average commission and MANA illustration (owner keeps ~30%) support modest economics. Founder's technical background fits design-in selling, but 6-24 month design cycles mean long unpaid ramp, unproven agencies get weak lines, and lines get pulled once developed. Territory-capped; relationship-heavy so hard to delegate.
red_flags: Signing 5-8 viable lines in 12 months assumed

rationale: Low-barrier, seasonal (May-Oct) commodity trade with many small operators and price-shopping property managers. Census op margin is a broad 238990 proxy. Satellite-measured proposals help speed but are easily copied. Deferrable spend in downturns; snow adjacency helps utilization. Realistic FCF ~$60-120k.

No spending or market-size data at all; economics entirely analyst estimates. Lumpy project revenue with thin maintenance recurrence, work-at-height risk, niche ceiling. Moderate competition and low capital make it a reasonable add-on to commercial pest control rather than a standalone base.

Shrinking independent retail, small orders, and Faire-type marketplaces disintermediating reps. Commission rate (~15%) unverified; payment often 60-90+ days after retailer pays. Author's own range $0-70k and $10k/mo ceiling. Founder-relationship bound; discretionary demand.

Best demand evidence in packet: 1,779 Chicago tuckpointing permits at $15k median plus public wall/parapet violations; Census masonry margin ~20% (incumbent). But founder lacks trade skill, needs a supervising licensed mason, scarce W-2 masons, heavy fall/insurance risk, seasonality, crowded field. Deposits help cash.
red_flags: Insurance cost for height work MISSING

rationale: Mandate is documented (NFPA 80 via 41 IAC 100.7) and healthcare accreditation pressure is real, but there is no spend, pricing or competitor data. Institutional buyers need vendor credentialing, net-45/90 pay, 1-6 month cycles; credibility without track record is the hurdle. Good adjacency line (dampers, firestopping).

Zebra partner program openly accessible and founder's tech background fits; label/ribbon consumables give recurrence. But hardware margins thin (10-20%), established AIDC VARs and Amazon for ribbons, and large accounts buy from national VARs. Only incumbent/distributor financials cited; small-VAR margins are estimates.
red_flags: Conversion from consumables to projects assumed

rationale: Chicago requires electrical contractor license with supervising electrician even for low-voltage, or a state private alarm license with experience requirement; founder must hire licensed staff. Crowded, equipment float, net-30-60 plus retainage. IES data-center growth is incumbent and not this segment.
red_flags: Incumbent segment data not relevant to small retrofits

rationale: Durable essential demand and active consolidators (Service Logic) show long-run value, but founder cannot service equipment and must recruit scarce experienced techs from day one; PM is near-breakeven, profit depends on repair pull-through. Higher capital ($40-120k), crowded field, net-30/45. Pricing and margins are estimates.
red_flags: Tech recruitment in tight market assumed

rationale: Global Industrial economics are a scaled incumbent with in-stock margins; a new niche site faces paid-search CAC of 8-15%, MAP/online-gating, and Amazon/Grainger/Zoro. Founder's tech skills fit and cash cycle can be favorable, but author's own yr3 range starts at $0. Platform/ad dependence weakens resilience.

Strong public evidence: ~2,000 porch/stair violations and 473 express porch permits ($10k median) in 2025; owners identifiable and deadline-motivated. Light Chicago GC license. But founder lacks carpentry, needs lead carpenters; Chicago-only building type caps scale; structural liability and owner payment delays. Specialist wedge copyable.

No sources at all; spend, pricing, and mandate adoption unverified. OEM generator dealers entrenched with institutional buyers; $40-120k load-bank capital; high-energy electrical safety and possible electrician licensing; founder must hire specialized techs. Demand itself is likely durable (healthcare, data centers).
red_flags: NFPA 110 adoption for IL healthcare unverified

rationale: Real small-lot niche below Univar/Brenntag MOQs and Census chemical-wholesaler margins (24% GM, ~8% op) support sector economics, but launch needs a compliant hazmat warehouse and drum inventory ($60-200k), producer access is unverified, and spill/compliance liability is heavy. Author's yr3 range starts at $0.
red_flags: Capital could exceed $100k pre-revenue at high end

rationale: Recurring, frequent need from identifiable property managers; asset-light with standard painter/handyman labor and crew-lead delegation. Census painting margins (incumbent) support economics; per-turn pricing and PM outsourcing share are missing. Wedge (SLA, fixed menu) is easily copied; net-30-45 portals and quality control are the key risks.

Dense Chicago logistics corridors and frequent forklift-damage repairs suggest real recurring demand, but no spend or pricing data (only CBP establishment counts). Founder must hire scarce experienced door techs; overhead-door dealers with manufacturer agreements compete; parts inventory and net-30/60 terms. No licensing barrier.

Buyers search by part number, and catalog-data skills fit the founder, but Parts Town-type incumbents and OEM portals dominate, OEM authorization is selective, and availability promise requires inventory with obsolescence risk. No niche demand evidence; author's yr3 range starts at $0.

New legal path is a genuine opening, but 2025 Chicago data show only ~165 ADU/coach-house permit mentions; long financing/permit cycles at 7%+ rates, one-off projects with fixed-price overrun risk, and plan permits require a licensed architect partner. Author's ceiling ~$10k/mo.
red_flags: Market too small per own permit data

rationale: Standalone roof PM competes with roofers who give inspections free to win replacements; requires Illinois roofing license (QP exam) and expensive fall/workers-comp insurance. No PM spend or pricing data, only CBP counts. Drone reporting is a modest, copyable wedge.

Price-transparent branded instruments, selective brand authorization, and Grainger/Transcat scale leave a newcomer 15-25% GM and no wedge; author's own entry strategy is 'weak' and yr3 range $0-60k. Transcat earns only 4% operating margin at scale.

Buyers identifiable from demolition/construction permits and recurring rent is attractive, but fleet capex upfront, theft/damage, GC net-30-60, and construction cyclicality. United Rentals/Herc margins are incumbent with cheap capital and density; fence pricing missing. Growth requires continual fleet reinvestment, depressing FCF.

Annual rebids make buyers accessible and the need is real in Chicago winters, but economics are weather-volatile, slip-and-fall liability and insurance are severe, subcontractor no-shows at 2am are common, and cash cycle is poor (salt pre-buys, subs paid before net-60/90 aggregator receipts). No snow-specific spend or pricing data.

Major lighting lines are held by entrenched agencies in exclusive territories; newcomers get second-tier lines, spec-to-ship 6-24 months, commissions months to years after spec, and serving specifiers requires staffed agencies. Only all-agent average commission cited. Author's yr3 range $0-100k.

Capital-heavy ($80-300k fleet, likely personal guarantees with unknown founder credit) against United Rentals/Herc/big-box competitors with density and cheap capital; at incumbent 38.5% dollar utilization a small yard keeps little after depreciation. No wedge; construction-cyclical; author ceiling ~$10k/mo.
red_flags: Incumbent EBITDA irrelevant to small yard

rationale: No sources. Entrenched firms, buyers require track and safety records, union labor and very high insurance, fatality risk that can end the company, $50-150k capital and 9-month time to revenue. Author's entry strategy is 'weak for newcomer'. Not a fit for a founder without rope-access experience.

Washes are easy to identify and chemicals are continuous consumables, but there is no industry, margin, or territory evidence; chemical brands likely appoint distributors by territory and PE-backed express chains increasingly buy nationally. Finite local customer count limits scale; inventory and vans needed.

Code-required inspections are durable, but reports need an Illinois-licensed PE partner and accredited lab, buyers use qualification-based selection favoring established firms, 9 months to first revenue, and 60-90 day public/owner receivables plus retainage. No testing-specific spend or pricing data.

Simple, highly delegable monthly route service with many small buyers and short cycles; low licensing burden; consolidators value recurring books. But nationals (Cintas, Rentokil) bundle with mats/uniforms, unit capex per account, small tickets ($50-250/month), and pricing/route revenue are analyst estimates only.

Health-code-driven recurring consumable with real switching costs once installed; Ecolab's 44.5% GM shows category value but is incumbent economics. Newcomer faces Ecolab/Auto-Chlor, dispenser capex stranded by restaurant failures, after-hours service burden; private-label chemistry access unverified. Delegable route-tech model.

Census masonry materials spend and SiteOne/BFS margins (~5% operating) show thin distribution economics even at scale; newcomer likely 2-6%. Needs $60-200k inventory/yard, contractor credit with slow payers, unverified manufacturer line cards, and contractors loyal to existing yards. Jobsite delivery wedge is weak.

Chicago-area data-center build-out is a plausible tailwind and specialist protocols give some wedge, but no sources at all: spend, pricing, and competitors missing. Buyers require security clearance and track record; construction cleans are lumpy with GC pay-when-paid (net-60+). Low capital.

Chefs' Warehouse (3.5% op margin) and grocery wholesaler data show very thin margins even at scale; new entrant needs $50-200k for imports, cold chain and inventory, faces spoilage, tariffs, FSVP compliance, and lacks the community ties that drive this niche. Author's yr3 range $0-100k.

Plant capex $250k-1.5M before revenue at a housing-cycle trough (BFS operating margin fell to 5.2%, single-family permits -12.9%); concentrated builders with incumbent suppliers; author marks it reject with no credible entry strategy. Fails capital gate.

Large pass-through revenue potential but 10-25% gross on subcontractor spend, severe negative float (subs paid in 15-30 days vs chains net-45/90) that grows with revenue, RFP-driven 3-12 month cycles, credibility walls, and scaled tech platforms (Lessen et al.). Software/AI automation real but incumbents have it too. Author's yr3 range starts at $0.

Outsider with no clinical/OR background cannot access surgeon relationships or credentialing; principals expect agencies to bring a surgeon book; incumbent reps hold non-competes; Anti-Kickback/Sunshine compliance sensitivity is high; principals take territories in-house after acquisitions. Commission rates unverified.

Chicago supply is small (3,712 registrations) and constrained by primary-residence rules, building caps and prohibited lists; third-party management may need a real-estate broker license (RELA exemption scope unverified). Platform-dependent, heavily competed, AI tools are commoditized. Author ceiling ~$10k/mo.

No sources at all. Plausible small niche with reachable high-rise managers and possibly thin competition, but low frequency (annual/semiannual), small dollars, unpleasant work, and author's own ceiling ~$10k/mo. Fine as an add-on to a building-services route, not a base business.

Spec-to-commission lag of 12-36 months means founder self-funds for years; value-engineering substitutions kill specs; project-based and construction-cyclical; only generic all-agent commission data. Many niche manufacturers will sign a rep, but economics depend on founder's personal spec-writer relationships. Author's yr3 range $0-80k.

Excellent public targeting data (50k violations at 10.8k addresses) and prepaid plan fees, but willingness of price-sensitive small landlords to pay recurring fees is entirely unproven; profit relies on repair work through subcontracted licensed trades. Chicago-only, abundant handyman competition, liability for missed hazards.

Commodity hourly labor resale with 15-30% gross margins, weekly payroll against net-30/60 receivables, extreme competition from nationals, RFP sales, and IDFPR private security contractor licensing that likely requires experience the founder lacks (needs licensed manager). CBP payroll data only; no viable wedge per author.
